Takes a little more than intro stats to get the 'correct' perspective and create the right takeaways. We're considering one variable (BMI) and one test (prediction of too much body fat) Let's start here:

  1. Classifying a pattern prediction method as common-speech 'inaccurate' or 'accurate' doesn't mean much technically
  2. What is the confidence of a 'positive' prediction?
  3. What is the occurrence of a false negative?

Using BMI for purpose (2) is very accurate (colloquial usage). Using BMI for purpose (3)is not very accurate. As an 'end user', here's what it means to you:

• If BMI says you're fat, you're fat • If BMI doesn't say you're fat, that doesn't give you enough information to determine if you're fat or not

So, if your BMI is over 30, you're irrefutably fat, barring some outlandish explanation (eg, if you're Dorian Yates).

The German health system works overall as you have described. The majority of people are under Public Health Insurance, which is run by non-profit organizations operating at cost, are forced to grant insurance to almost anyone and receive their fee as fixed percentage of your income, without differentiating by age, pre-conditions etc.

You can also get so-called Complimentary Private Health Insurance to receive special benefits on top of the basic public coverage like a guaranteed single room in hospital or extended dental options, which operate at profit and also have the right to turn you down or charge you an increased fee if you bring special risk factors such as age or obesity.

You can also opt out of public insurance and get Private Health Insurance at a at-profit company, and some people (such as public servants or entrepreneurs) are barred from public insurance and have to pick private insurance if they want health coverage. The problem is that once you opt out, it is next to impossible to switch to public insurance again. I know a lot of people who switched to private when they were young and were lured by the low fees for young people, and are now ass-fucked dry by the rapidly increasing fee for getting older.

There are still a lot of leeches, waste and cronyism (such as our drug store cartel), and I predict it will become much worse within a few decades as more and more leeches receiving free gibs are added to the health system, but our German system doesn't seem to be even a quarter as fucked up as the American health sector. The insurance is sold by private companies. These private companies compete against each other to fight over the market.

Competition between private companies fighting each other keeps the prices more efficient than any government or charity administration can do the job. Note - this is not a monopoly or oligopoly market situation - the market is not dominated by a few large insurance carriers.
